c.tagline: Canada's 'Birthplace of Confederation,' with Victorian streets and Anne of Green Gables lore nearby
langs: French (official Canadian second language, limited local use)

card: Widely accepted everywhere including tap-to-pay; cash rarely needed

taxi.fare: Metered, roughly CAD $3.50 flag fall plus per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Downtown is compact enough to walk; taxis mainly useful for the airport or beaches outside town

emergency.note: 911 reaches police, fire, and ambulance across Canada

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Downtown Charlottetown is compact and very walkable; a car or tour is useful for Cavendish, Green Gables, or PEI's north-shore beaches

safety.safety: Very safe small city with low crime and a relaxed pace
safety.crime: Petty theft is rare; violent crime is uncommon

hood_desc: The historic waterfront core with Province House, museums, and the marina; the natural base for most visitors.
A closed-to-traffic block of restaurant patios and boutiques just off the main downtown grid, lively on summer evenings.
An affluent, tree-lined Victorian neighborhood west of downtown with grand heritage homes; good for a quieter, walkable stay.
A quiet residential area near the university, suited to longer stays or those wanting a local, non-touristy feel.
A suburban commercial strip with shopping centers and chain hotels, convenient for drivers and budget travelers.

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality.

transit.hours: Roughly 6:30am-9pm on weekdays, reduced weekend service
transit.pay: Cash fare or day pass on board
transit.note: Downtown is best explored on foot; a car is recommended for exploring the rest of PEI

transport.air: Charlottetown Airport (YYG), about 10 min from downtown
transport.train: No passenger rail service on Prince Edward Island
transport.bus: Maritime Bus connects Charlottetown to Moncton and onward to the rest of the Maritimes
transport.ferry: Northumberland Ferries seasonal service to Nova Scotia from Wood Islands
transport.car: Confederation Bridge links PEI to New Brunswick; a car is the easiest way to explore the island

airport.name: Charlottetown Airport
airport.transport: Taxi, rental car, or hotel shuttle

net.m: Good 4G/5G coverage in the city, patchier in rural PEI
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ap: A Canadian prepaid SIM or eSIM

landmarks: Province House National Historic Site
The neoclassical sandstone legislature where the 1864 Charlottetown Conference launched Canadian Confederation, earning the city its 'Birthplace of Canada' title.
Confederation Centre of the Arts
Canada's memorial to Confederation stages the long-running Anne of Green Gables musical and houses an art gallery celebrating the nation's creators.
St. Dunstan's Basilica
Twin Gothic spires of this grand 1919 stone basilica dominate the skyline, sheltering a soaring fan-vaulted interior rare in the Maritimes.
Victoria Row
A brick-paved pedestrian block of Victorian storefronts where patios, buskers, and galleries create Charlottetown's liveliest summer streetscape beside the Confederation Centre.
Peake's Wharf and the Waterfront Boardwalk
The historic harborfront where Confederation delegates landed now buzzes with ice-cream shops, boat tours, and strolls along Charlottetown Harbour.
Victoria Park
Forty waterside acres of old-growth trees, the 1805 Prince Edward Battery cannons, and a boardwalk beloved for sunsets over the harbor entrance.
Great George Street
The National Historic District avenue linking harbor to Province House, lined with heritage inns and churches, walked by the Fathers of Confederation in 1864.
Beaconsfield Historic House
An elegant 1877 Victorian mansion of gingerbread trim and harbor views, preserved as a museum of Prince Edward Island's gilded shipbuilding era.
Green Gables Heritage Place (Cavendish)
A half-hour drive away, the green-gabled farmhouse that inspired Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of Green Gables enchants pilgrims with Lover's Lane and Haunted Wood trails.
Confederation Landing Park
Manicured waterfront lawns mark the very spot where the Fathers of Confederation stepped ashore in 1864, ideal for picnics beside the marina.

train.note: Prince Edward Island has no railway - the last trains ran in 1989 and the trackbed is now the Confederation Trail. Arrive across the Confederation Bridge by coach or car, on the Wood Islands ferry, or by air. The nearest VIA Rail station is Moncton, New Brunswick, about three hours away.

bus.note: No international coaches. Maritime Bus (https://www.maritimebus.com/) is the regional operator, running from Charlottetown to Moncton in about 3h30, Halifax (5h30) and Summerside, crossing the Confederation Bridge. Services run roughly once or twice a day, so plan around the timetable; T3 Transit covers the city.

intl.to: Caribou, Nova Scotia (Canada) - sails from Wood Islands, ~1 hr from Charlottetown, ~75 min crossing, May-Dec

ferry.note: There are no international sailings. The Wood Islands to Caribou ferry is a genuine alternative to the Confederation Bridge for reaching Nova Scotia and is the more scenic route, but it operates only from about May to late December and the terminal is an hour's drive southeast of Charlottetown. You pay only when leaving the island. Reservations are recommended in summer for vehicles.

half.name: Prince Edward Island National Park
half.blurb: Red sandstone cliffs, dunes and beaches along the island's north shore, a short drive from the capital.

half.name: Basin Head Beach
half.blurb: A remote eastern-shore beach famous for its singing sands that squeak underfoot, plus a fisheries heritage museum nearby.

half.name: Souris
half.blurb: A working fishing harbor town on the island's east coast, gateway to the Northumberland Strait ferry to the Magdalen Islands.

full.name: Nova Scotia (via Wood Islands ferry)
full.blurb: A ferry crossing to Pictou County on the mainland, giving access to Nova Scotia's coastal towns and lighthouses for the day.
